newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan opposition says 500 killed in fall of town.
newsitem.headline: Afghan opposition says 500 killed in fall of town.

text.p: Forces loyal to Afghanistan's anti-Taleban alliance on Sunday claimed a major rout of Taleban forces in fierce fighting with heavy casualties north of Kabul during the night.

At midday on Sunday, a lone aircraft flew over Kabul and dropped bombs near the city's main airport, killing at least seven people and injuring 12 in a two-storey house in the suburb of Khair Khana, residents said. An earlier raid near the airport caused no casualties or damage and the bombs landed outside the field's perimeter, an official said.
In the overnight fighting, the opposition took the town of Charikar, 65 km (40 miles) north of Kabul on Saturday night, and nearby Bagram airbase on Sunday morning, a senior opposition official said.
Charikar controls access to the Ghorband valley, where the Taleban are fighting forces of the Hezb-e-Wahdat faction, a mainly Shi'ite party which is a member of the opposition alliance.
Bagram airbase was Kabul's main military air field, but has been out of action for 10 months as it was too close to the front line.

"We captured Charikar at 9 P.M. (1630 GMT) on Saturday night, and Bagram airbase at 9 this morning (0430 GMT). We closed the road and the Taleban could not withdraw any of their vehicles or equipment," an official of the government ousted from Kabul last September told Reuters on Sunday.
He said that 500 Taleban fighters had been killed in the battle.
The official, who wanted to remain anonymous, was speaking by satellite telephone from the Panjsher valley, stronghold of the ex-government's senior military commander Ahmed Shah Masood.
There was no confirmation of his reports, but journalists who tried to reach the area on Sunday morning were turned back by Taleban fighters.
A Taleban official, speaking from their base in the southern Afghan city of Kandahar, said that he had no information on the opposition claims.
Charikar fell to the Taleban in January, but the town has been under pressure from opposition forces for more than a month since they took the town of Jabal os-Siraj 70 km (45 miles) north of Kabul.
The Taleban have been under continuous pressure since they briefly captured most of the opposition-held north of the country in May.

They lost the area after only four days and have been gradually losing ground ever since. But they still control more than three quarters of Afghanistan, including the capital, and are the most formidable force in the country.
In Sunday's midday air raid, a witness said most of the dead and wounded came from the house directly hit in the attack where the owner was hosting lunch for friends and relatives.
As the aircraft flew over the capital, Taleban guns erupted with anti-aircraft fire, but the thumps of the bombs exploding all but drowned out the chatter of small arms fire.

Kabul airport is used for both military and civilian traffic and has been frequently targetted in the past. Both the International Committee of the Red Cross and the United Nations use it for the transport of staff and supplies. Both agencies had planes land between the morning and midday raids on Sunday.
